Listen to this article Share …Umahi orders three-week nationwide emergency road repairs ahead of festive rush, 2027 polls Advertisement Advertisement The Federal Government is seeking to turn the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway into a revenue-generating infrastructure asset, exploring carbon credit monetisation and private-sector investments to recover construction costs amid mounting pressure on public finances. David Umahi, minister of works, disclosed this during an inspection of bridge construction along Sections 1 and 2 of the 750-kilometre highway, saying the government intends to leverage the project’s concrete pavement, solar-powered streetlights and proposed commercial developments to attract climate finance and private capital. The government is also considering industrial parks, tourism facilities and other commercial developments along the corridor as part of efforts to improve its economic viability. Addressing concerns over project continuity and competing fiscal priorities, Umahi stated that the administration remains locked in on delivering the entire stretch across Nigeria’s nine coastal states, noting that ongoing reconstruction of the East-West Road is a parallel commitment rather than a replacement. “Nothing will happen to the 750-kilometre Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, which passes through the nine coastal states. The President has directed that the project must be completed as envisaged,” Umahi said. Advertisement He said that beyond easing logistics along the southern littoral corridor, the Ministry of Works is structuring the highway to tap into international climate finance and private equity. According to Umahi, the adoption of continuous reinforced concrete pavement alongside solar-powered street lighting qualifies the project for carbon credit claims, a revenue stream the government intends to leverage alongside private investor buy-ins. Advertisement “We are using concrete, and so we are entitled to carbon credits claim. We are also using solar instead of conventional electricity; we are entitled to carbon credits,” the minister explained, adding that private investors have already signalled interest in recouping construction costs through structured investment arrangements. The corridor is also being designed as an economic zone capable of hosting industrial parks, tourism hubs, and integrated CCTV surveillance infrastructure. Alongside the coastal route, Umahi highlighted the 1,068-kilometre Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway as a twin pillar of the administration’s long-term logistics masterplan. Advertisement Advertisement In a separate directive aimed at de-risking year-end supply chains and pre-election logistics, Umahi ordered a three-week emergency rehabilitation blitz across critical federal highways spanning all six geopolitical zones. He ordered zonal directors, federal controllers, resident engineers, and contractors to mobilise immediately to patch failed sections ahead of the December festive travel surge and the January 2027 general elections. Umahi criticised contractors executing long-term construction contracts while leaving adjacent carriageways impassable for commuters and haulage operators, ordering the immediate excavation and asphalt reinstatement of critical bottlenecks. “I feel so sad that a contractor will be on site doing permanent work, yet some sections of the roads remain impassable. This practice must stop,” he warned, directing ministry field officers to document compliance and escalate bottlenecks within the 21-day window to guarantee seamless movement of goods, election materials, and security personnel.
